9.4 — Your Scene Is Data: Metadata & Files

Every Unity scene you have saved is a text file. So is every Inspector value you have dragged, every [SerializeField] you have written. Today you open the black box: your game is data all the way down, and reading that data changes how you think about both Unity AND the exam's "data abstraction" questions.

Concept Lab ~15 min

Step 1 — see the scene. In your project folder, find Assets/Scenes/Platformer.unity. Open it in a TEXT editor (TextEdit, VS Code — not Unity). It is YAML, a human-readable key: value format:

--- !u!1 &123456789
GameObject:
  m_ObjectHideFlags: 0
  m_Name: Turret
  m_TagString: Untagged
  m_Component:
  - component: {fileID: 22400000}
--- !u!212 &987654321
SpriteRenderer:
  m_Sprite: {fileID: 21300000, guid: a1b2c3..., type: 3}
  m_Color: {r: 1, g: 1, b: 1, a: 1}

Find YOUR turret by name in the text. Its maxAttackRange, its attackCooldown — the numbers you tuned in the Inspector all semester — are stored right here, as text, in a file. The Inspector was never magic; it is a YAML editor with better styling.

Step 2 — the .meta files. Every asset has an assetname.png.meta. Open one: a guid (a globally unique ID), import settings, dimensions. THIS is how a scene references a sprite without a file path — by guid, not by name. Delete a .meta and its asset loses every Inspector connection it ever had (the classic "everything went pink" disaster).

Step 3 — serialization is the exam word. [SerializeField] private float speed — Unity SERIALIZIZES the field: converts the C# object's state into text/YAML for storage, and back on load. That is literally what the exam means by serialization in Unit 9's data-in-transit questions:

your code (memory)  --serialize-->  the .unity file (disk)
the file (disk)     --deserialize--> your fields at runtime

Socratic

Prefabs (2.4) are YAML too. Explain "prefab as data abstraction": what does a prefab FILE hide, and what does its guid GUARANTEE that a file path cannot (hint: rename a sprite and count what breaks — then rename a file that is referenced by guid and count again)?

Build Lab ~20 min

Step 1 — break a scene with a text edit. (Copy the file first!) In the .unity text, find your turret's maxAttackRange line and change 7 to 20. Close Unity first (it caches), reopen, press Play. The change is THERE — you edited the game without ever opening the Inspector. Same power as the palette edit from 9.2, one level deeper.

Step 2 — diff a playtest edit. Make a copy of Platformer.unity, then in Unity move three objects. Save. Diff the two files (VS Code's compare, or just search for the changed numbers). Each moved object = a few changed m_LocalPosition values. Your whole semester of design edits is THIS readable.

Step 3 — a save system, previewed. Your game keeps coins in a scene-local StatManager singleton — a reload forgets (which is the arcade design you defended in 8.5). But now you KNOW how saves work: serialize the fields you care about (coins, hasAxe, maxJumps) to a text file (JSON is YAML's cousin), deserialize on boot. That is PlayerPrefs or a JSON file — and it is the Create PT's "data" requirement, live in your own game.

Bug Hunt: Text-edit disasters

  1. Break one YAML indentation (delete two spaces before a key). What does Unity say when the scene loads? Why do data formats care about STRUCTURE, not just content?
  2. Change the turret's sprite guid to a random guid you typed. What goes pink — and why did a guid (not a name) break it (what did you learn about guids in Step 2)?
  3. Rename a sprite's FILE but not the .meta. Open Unity. Nothing broke — explain why the .meta is the actual identity and the filename is a costume.
  4. You edited the scene text while Unity was OPEN. What happened to your edit — and why is "close before edit" not just superstition (what does Unity hold in memory and write back)?
Tinker ~10 min

Tinker: Data everywhere

  1. AP practice: "Which of the following is a benefit of storing data in a documented text format rather than a binary format?" — write TWO answers (human readability; diff/version history) with your scene diff as evidence.
  2. Your playtest tables (7.7) are CSV — is CSV a serialization format? What does it serialize, what does it leave out (types!) — and why is "typeless" both its charm and its danger?
  3. Hard: JSON-write your player's run summary (coins, deaths, time) with JsonUtility.ToJson. One line. What does the string look like — and why does it look EXACTLY like the YAML you read today?

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Open a scene/prefab as text and find a specific object's data
  • Explain [SerializeField] as serialization both directions
  • Explain guid references and why renames do not break them
  • Sketch a save system as serialize → file → deserialize
